'''Ray Hilborn''' (born 1947) is a [[marine biologist]] and [[fisheries scientist]], known for his work on conservation and [[natural resource management]] in the context of [[fisheries]]. He is currently professor of aquatic and fishery science at the [[University of Washington]]. He focuses on conservation, natural resource management, fisheries stock assessment and risk analysis, and advises several international fisheries commissions and agencies.<ref name="Hilborn">[http://www.fish.washington.edu/people/rayh/index.html Ray Hilborn] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207163608/http://www.fish.washington.edu/people/rayh/index.html |date=2010-02-07 }}</ref><ref>[http://www.worldcat.org/identities/lccn-n86-805296 Hilborn, Ray 1947- ] ''WorldCat Identities''. Retrieved 15 November 2012.</ref>
  
==Biography==
Ray Hilborn has authored more than 200 peer-reviewed scientific papers, and several books.

In 1992, Hilborn coauthored ''Quantitative fisheries stock assessment'' with Carl Walters. In 1997, he coauthored ''The Ecological Detective: Confronting Models with Data'' with Marc Mangel. In 2012, he coauthored ''Overfishing: what everyone needs to know'' with Ulrike Hilborn.

With [[Carl Walters]], he jointly received the [[Wildlife Society]] award for best paper in fish ecology and management, ''Adaptive control of fishing systems''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Walters |first1=Carl J. |last2=Hilborn |first2=Ray |title=Adaptive Control of Fishing Systems |journal=Journal of the Fisheries Research Board of Canada |date=1976 |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=145–159 |doi=10.1139/f76-017 |s2cid=53723411 |url=http://www.iiasa.ac.at/Admin/PUB/Documents/WP-75-114.pdf }}</ref>

In 2006, he shared the [[Volvo Environment Prize]] with [[Daniel Pauly]] and [[Carl Walters]].<ref>[http://www.environment-prize.com/ The Volvo Environment Prize ... - Volvo Environment Prize<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> He is a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Canada]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. Ray Hilborn |publisher=Royal Society of Canada |url=https://rsc-src.ca/en/find-rsc-member/results?combine=&first_name=Ray&last_name=Hilborn&current_employer=&academy_25=All&is_deceased=All }}</ref>

In 2011, he received the [[Ecological Society of America]]'s [[Sustainability science|Sustainability Science]] Award for a 2009 paper with [[Boris Worm]] and others<ref>{{cite web |title=Sustainability Science Award |url=https://www.esa.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/94/2022/02/sustain2011.pdf |publisher=Ecological Society of America}}</ref> entitled ''Rebuilding global fisheries''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Worm |first1=Boris |last2=Hilborn |first2=Ray |display-authors=etal |title=Rebuilding global fisheries |journal=Science |date=2009 |volume=325 |issue=5940 |pages=578–585 |doi=10.1126/science.1173146|pmid=19644114 |bibcode=2009Sci...325..578W |s2cid=2805799 |hdl=11336/100063 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

In 2016 he received the International Fisheries Science Prize at the World Fisheries Congress in Busan, South Korea. The award recognized his 40-year career of "highly diversified research and publication in support of global fisheries science and conservation," according to a news release.

His major areas of current and past research interest include "Bayesian analysis of decision making in natural resources, [[adaptive management]] of renewable resources, the dynamics of the Serengeti ecosystem in east Africa, the role of hatcheries in management of Pacific salmon, the ability of institutions to learn from experience, statistical methods in testing dynamic ecological hypotheses, the analysis of migration and dispersal from mark–recapture data, and the ecological dynamics of fishing fleets."<ref name="Hilborn"/>

==Fisheries management research==
In their research, Hilborn and Walters investigated the ways that dynamic models can be used to manage fisheries in order to maintain states of optimum equilibrium. In their paper,<ref>Adaptive Control of Fishing Systems. 1975</ref> they examined the effectiveness of using the [[Ricker model|Ricker]] and [[Beverton-Holt model]]s models to estimate the potential yield of future generations by using data taken from prior generations. They addressed the problem that, in regards to fisheries, the parameters of the control system are often either varied or uncertain and the use of historical data becomes progressively more unreliable as it gets older. Variables, regarding these issues, include natural mortality and spawning rates as well the effects of human fishing, as a predator-prey relationship. Influenced by [[control theory]], Hilborn and Walters modified the original models with various new formulae to create alternative models, in order to achieve more accurate predictions. They then identified "a series of alternative harvesting experiments… each of which would be reasonably certain to discriminate between the alternative models…"<ref>Walters, Carl; Hilborn, Ray (September 1975). "Adaptive Control of Fishing Systems": 19.</ref> The development of these alternative models and harvesting methods has been invaluable in assessing the sustainability of the world's fisheries.

Hilborn's research "aims to identify how to best manage fisheries to provide sustainable benefits to human society. This involves a combination of building data bases on how fisheries are managed and measures of their performance."<ref>{{cite web |title=Ray Hilborn |publisher=UW School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences |url=https://fish.uw.edu/faculty/ray-hilborn/}}</ref> He has contributed extensively to The Ram Legacy database<ref>{{cite web |url=http://ramlegacy.org// |title=RAM Legacy Stock Assessment Database}}</ref> which "provides estimates of status indicators such as biomass, fishing mortality rates, and associated reference points, and is the most quantitatively robust source of fishery status available."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hilborn |first1=Ray |last2=Ovando |first2=Daniel |title=Reflections on the success of traditional fisheries management |journal=ICES Journal of Marine Science |date=2014 |volume=71 |issue=5 |pages=1040–1046 |doi=10.1093/icesjms/fsu034|doi-access=free }}</ref> Hilborn's efforts attempt to strike a balance between resource sustainability for the environment and food and nutrition security for human beings. When it comes to large scale management of fisheries, he contends that there is "no single solution, and what is appropriate for one community for a specific species may be totally different for another species or community"<ref>Hilborn, Ray. "Knowledge on How To Achieve Sustainable Fisheries": 53.</ref> According to Hilborn, successful management strategies involve a combination of limiting access to fisheries, maintaining biological productivity and the cooperation of all stakeholders involved.

==Controversy==
In 2016 in a publicly posted 8-page letter to the President of the University of Washington, Greenpeace USA accused Dr. Hilborn of conflict of interest in the conduct of his research about the effects of fishing on the health of fish populations.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hocevar |first1=John |title=Letter to the University of Washington |url=https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/2830296-Greenpeace-Hilborn-Complaint-Letter.html |website=Greenpeace USA }}</ref>  Greenpeace alleged that undisclosed research and consulting funding provided to Dr. Hilborn from the seafood industry had influenced his research.  Hilborn denied the charges and was cleared after formal investigation by the University of Washington.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bernton |first1=Hal |title=UW backs fishery professor in research dispute with Greenpeace |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/education/uw-backs-fishery-prof-in-research-dispute-with-greenpeace/ |access-date=April 30, 2020 |publisher=Seattle Times |date=June 22, 2016}}</ref>

In October 2017 the [[NOAA]] Assistant Administrator for Fisheries wrote an open letter to the journal ''[[Marine Policy]]'' <ref name=Han2017>{{Cite web|url=https://retractionwatch.com/2017/11/06/senior-noaa-appointee-calls-retraction-paper-illegal-fishing/|title=Senior NOAA appointee calls for retraction of paper on illegal fishing|last=Han|first=Andrew|date=November 6, 2017|website=Retraction Watch|access-date=January 25, 2019}}</ref> about a published paper co-authored by [[Tony J. Pitcher]] which suggested the U.S. exports to Japan a significant amount of seafood products from [[illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing]] (IUU).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pramod |first1=Ganapathiraju |last2=Pitcher |first2=Tony J. |last3=Mantha |first3=Gopikrishna |title=RETRACTED: Estimates of illegal and unreported seafood imports to Japan |journal=Marine Policy |date=2017 |volume=84 |pages=42–51 |doi=10.1016/j.marpol.2017.06.032|doi-access=free |bibcode=2017MarPo..84...42P }}{{Retracted|doi=10.1016/j.marpol.2019.103574|http://retractionwatch.com/2019/01/12/weekend-reads-fishy-research-on-fishes-was-sokal-squared-misconduct-the-misuse-of-metrics/ ''Retraction Watch''|intentional=yes}}</ref> The NOAA letter said it "strongly objects to the authors' claims regarding U.S. seafood exports to Japan and doubts the validity of the methodology used to make such estimates."<ref name=Han2017 /> In January 2019, ''Marine Policy'' had retracted the study,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.intrafish.com/fisheries/1670981/controversial-iuu-science-paper-finally-retracted|title=Controversial IUU science paper finally retracted|last=Fiorillo|first=John|date=January 10, 2019|website=IntraFish|access-date=January 25, 2019}}</ref> and the article was formally retracted by the editor of ''Marine Policy'' in September 2019.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Retraction Notice to "Estimates of illegal and unreported seafood imports to Japan" |journal=Marine Policy |date=2019 |volume=107 |doi=10.1016/j.marpol.2019.103574|last1=Pramod |first1=Ganapathiraju |last2=Pitcher |first2=Tony J. |last3=Mantha |first3=Gopikrishna |article-number=103574 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019MarPo.10703574P }}</ref> The following month a revised version of the article was published in the same journal.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ganapathiraju |first1=Pramod |last2=Pitcher |first2=Tony J. |last3=Mantha |first3=Gopikrishna |title=Estimates of illegal and unreported seafood imports to Japan |journal=Marine Policy |date=2019 |volume=108 |page=103439 |doi=10.1016/j.marpol.2019.02.011|bibcode=2019MarPo.10803439G }}</ref> In the same issue Ray Hilborn ''et al''. contested the credibility of the estimates in the revised paper, on the grounds that, "their estimates are not substantiated by any known facts from the fishery".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hilborn |first1=Ray |last2=Anderson |first2=Christopher M. |last3=Kruse |first3=Gordon H. |last4=Punt |first4=Andre E. |last5=Sissenwine |first5=Michael |last6=Oliver |first6=Chris |last7=Ianelli |first7=James N. |last8=Trumble |first8=Robert J. |last9=Agnew |first9=David J. |last10=Baker |first10=Nicole |title=Pramod et al. methods to estimate IUU are not credible |journal=Marine Policy |date=2019 |volume=108 |article-number=103632 |doi=10.1016/j.marpol.2019.103632|bibcode=2019MarPo.10803632H |s2cid=201368720 }}</ref> Pitcher ''et al.'' countered by saying that instead of relying solely on public
